explanation: Farrukhsiyar's farman of 1717, won by John Surman's mission after Company surgeon William Hamilton cured the emperor, let the Company trade duty-free in Bengal for an annual payment of Rs 3,000 — Indian officials called it the Company's 'Magna Carta'. Bahadur Shah and Shah Alam are later Mughals, and Jahangir's 1613 concession was to Surat, not Bengal.

A dastak was the free pass issued under the 1717 farman that let goods move without paying transit duty; Company servants misused it for their own private trade, and Mir Qasim's abolition of inland duties in 1763 to end that abuse led straight to the Battle of Buxar.

The Associated Press of India, founded by K. C. Roy (sources vary between 1905 and 1910), is counted as India's first news agency; Reuters absorbed it in 1919 and it later merged into PTI in 1949. The Free Press of India, set up by S. Sadanand in 1927, was the first Indian-owned nationalist agency but came two decades later.

Persian was the official court language of the Mughals from Akbar's reign until the British replaced it in 1837; Urdu grew out of the camp-and-bazaar mixing of Persian with Khari Boli and became a court language only in the late Mughal twilight.

The Ilbert Bill (1883), drafted under Ripon by law member C. P. Ilbert, sought to let Indian judges try Europeans in the mofussil — a purely judicial question. The white settlers' agitation forced its dilution and taught educated Indians the value of organisation, feeding into the Congress's birth in 1885.

M. A. Jinnah put forward his Fourteen Points in March 1929 at a Muslim League meeting in Delhi, as the League's counter to the Nehru Report of 1928 which had rejected separate electorates and one-third Muslim representation at the Centre.

Henry Louis Vivian Derozio, teacher at Hindu College from 1826 until his dismissal in 1831, inspired the radical Young Bengal group that attacked orthodoxy and idolatry through papers like Parthenon and the Jnananvesan.

Gopal Hari Deshmukh wrote under the pen-name 'Lokahitawadi' in the Marathi weekly Prabhakar from 1848, his Shatapatre (hundred letters) attacking caste and priestly domination. Atmaram Pandurang is remembered instead as founder of the Prarthana Samaj (1867).

M. N. Roy founded the Communist Party of India at Tashkent in October 1920 and was the only Indian to sit on the Comintern's presidium, which is why he is called the pioneer of Indian communism. Nalini Gupta and Shaukat Usmani were his emissaries; S. A. Dange belonged to the later Kanpur (1925) group.

George V announced the transfer of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi at the Delhi Durbar of 12 December 1911, the same occasion at which the 1905 partition of Bengal was annulled. The actual shift of offices and the inauguration of New Delhi came much later, in 1912 and 1931 respectively.

B. R. Ambedkar launched the Independent Labour Party in Bombay in August 1936 to fight the 1937 provincial elections, where it won 15 of the 17 seats it contested; he later converted it into the Scheduled Castes Federation in 1942.

Dadabhai Naoroji propounded the drain theory, developed from the 1860s and set out fully in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901). R. C. Dutt's Economic History of India elaborated the argument but did not originate it.

Ajanta (Maharashtra, 2nd century BCE to 6th century CE) and Ellora are rock-cut cave complexes, and their murals — the Bodhisattva Padmapani at Ajanta, for instance — are the classic surviving examples of Indian cave painting. Pahari and Mysore are later miniature schools.
Bhangra is the Punjabi harvest dance performed at Baisakhi in April when the rabi wheat crop is cut, danced to the dhol; its women's counterpart is Giddha.
The Bhagavad Gita is 700 verses inside the Bhishma Parva of the Mahabharata, spoken by Krishna to Arjuna on the field of Kurukshetra just before the war begins.

The Lucknow Congress of December 1916 is usually taken as Gandhi's real entry into Indian political life after his 1915 return — it was there that Rajkumar Shukla persuaded him to take up the Champaran indigo cultivators' cause. The question is loosely worded, though: if 'practically appeared' means the moment he took command of the Congress, that was the Calcutta special session of September 1920 (non-cooperation resolution) confirmed at Nagpur in December 1920.

The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931 in Delhi: civil disobedience was suspended, most political prisoners released, and Gandhi agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference in London later that year. March 1930 is the trap — that is when the Dandi March began, not when the pact was made.
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel earned the title 'Iron Man of India' for integrating over 550 princely states into the Union as the first Home Minister in 1947-49, including the police action in Hyderabad.

Seclusion of women existed earlier but became widespread and socially prescribed among the north Indian upper classes under the Mughals, when court custom and imitation by Hindu aristocracy spread it. The Sultanate period is a defensible alternative since the practice entered India with Turkish rule, so the question turns on 'widespread' rather than 'introduced'.

Anil Kumar Sinha, a 1979-batch Bihar cadre IPS officer, took charge as CBI Director on 3 December 2014 and served till December 2016, so he was the sitting Director when this 2016 paper was set. This is a dated current-affairs item whose 'correct' answer depends on the exam date.
Patricia Scotland was chosen Secretary-General of the Commonwealth at the CHOGM in Malta in November 2015 and took office in April 2016 — the first woman to hold the post, succeeding Kamalesh Sharma.
Mauricio Macri, the centre-right mayor of Buenos Aires, won Argentina's first-ever presidential run-off in November 2015 and was sworn in on 10 December 2015, ending twelve years of Kirchner rule.

In November 2015 China announced the world's largest animal cloning facility at Tianjin, a Boyalife joint venture with South Korea's Sooam Biotech, planned to produce cloned cattle, racehorses and pet dogs on an industrial scale.

The National Food Security Act, 2013 covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population — about two-thirds of India — with 5 kg of grain per person per month at Rs 3/2/1 for rice, wheat and coarse grains.
Seychelles joined the WTO on 26 April 2015 as its 161st member, after a twenty-year accession negotiation begun in 1995. Iran remains only an observer and North Korea is not a member at all.

ISIL stands for Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant — 'the Levant' being the English rendering of al-Sham, the eastern Mediterranean region covering Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Palestine; the alternative translation of al-Sham as 'Syria' gives the form ISIS.

Gunmen attacked the Paris office of the satirical weekly Charlie Hebdo on 7 January 2015, killing 12 including editor Stephane Charbonnier, over its caricatures of the Prophet; the slogan 'Je suis Charlie' followed.

The first English factory was set up at Surat in 1613, after Captain Best's naval victory over the Portuguese at Swally (1612) and Jahangir's permission; Sir Thomas Roe's 1615-19 embassy then secured wider trading rights. Hooghly (1651), Bombay (1668) and Calcutta (1690) all came later.

Robert Clive set up the Dual Government of Bengal in 1765 after obtaining the Diwani from Shah Alam II: the Company took revenue collection while the Nawab kept nizamat (law and order) — power without responsibility, and it ended in the famine of 1770. Warren Hastings abolished it in 1772.

The Mahalwari settlement, begun by Holt Mackenzie in 1822 and revised by R. M. Bird and James Thomason in 1833, assessed revenue on the mahal or whole village through its headmen, and covered the North-Western Provinces (western UP), Punjab and the Delhi territory. Bengal was under the Permanent Settlement and Madras under Ryotwari.

James Augustus Hicky brought out the Bengal Gazette (or Calcutta General Advertiser) in January 1780, India's first printed newspaper; its attacks on Warren Hastings got Hicky jailed and the paper seized in 1782.
Curzon's partition of Bengal was announced in July 1905 and took effect on 16 October 1905, which was observed as a day of mourning and rakhi-tying; it was annulled at the Delhi Durbar in 1911.

The Moplah (Mappila) rebellion of August 1921 broke out in the Malabar region of northern Kerala, mainly Ernad and Valluvanad taluks of Malappuram, where Muslim tenants rose against Hindu jenmi landlords amid the Khilafat-Non-Cooperation agitation.

Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana — 'Saubhagya' — was launched on 25 September 2017 to give free electricity connections to every un-electrified household. Ujjwala is the LPG-connection scheme and AMRUT is urban infrastructure, so both are near-miss distractors.

Brahmagupta, in the Brahmasphutasiddhanta of 628 CE, was the first to treat zero as a number and state rules for arithmetic with it and with negative quantities. Aryabhata used a place-value system with a zero placeholder but did not give the operational rules.

Swami Dayanand Saraswati, founder of the Arya Samaj (1875) and author of Satyarth Prakash, gave the call 'Back to the Vedas', holding the Vedas infallible and rejecting idolatry, caste by birth and later Puranic accretions.

Lord Dufferin was Viceroy when the Indian National Congress held its first session at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, in December 1885 under A. O. Hume's initiative; Dufferin himself later dismissed it as representing a 'microscopic minority'.

The Ghadar Party was founded at San Francisco in 1913 by Sohan Singh Bhakna as president and Lala Har Dayal as secretary, publishing the paper Ghadar; its planned 1915 rising in Punjab was betrayed and crushed. 1915 is the trap — that is the failed revolt, not the founding.

Dadabhai Naoroji, the 'Grand Old Man of India', first argued the drain of wealth in the 1860s-70s and set it out in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901), estimating the annual transfer to Britain through home charges and remittances.
Womesh Chunder Bonnerjee presided over the first Congress session in Bombay, December 1885. A. O. Hume was the founder and general secretary, not president — the standard trap here.

Lord Curzon issued the partition order in July 1905, splitting Bengal into a Muslim-majority Eastern Bengal and Assam and the rest, ostensibly for administrative convenience but in effect dividing nationalist Bengal; it triggered the Swadeshi movement.

The Swaraj Party was formed on 1 January 1923 by C. R. Das as president and Motilal Nehru as secretary, after the Gaya Congress rejected their plea to contest council elections following the withdrawal of Non-Cooperation. Of the four names given, only Motilal Nehru was a founder.

The Purna Swaraj resolution was adopted at the Lahore session of December 1929 under Jawaharlal Nehru's presidency; the tricolour was hoisted on the Ravi's bank on 31 December and 26 January 1930 was observed as the first Independence Day.

General Dyer's troops fired on an unarmed Baisakhi-day gathering at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar on 13 April 1919, protesting the Rowlatt Act and the arrest of Satyapal and Saifuddin Kitchlew; the Hunter Committee followed and Tagore returned his knighthood.

The AICC passed the Quit India resolution at Gowalia Tank, Bombay, on 8 August 1942, where Gandhi gave the 'Do or Die' call; the entire leadership was arrested in Operation Zero Hour in the early hours of 9 August.

The Interim Government took office on 2 September 1946 with Jawaharlal Nehru as Vice-President of the Viceroy's Executive Council; the Muslim League stayed out at first and joined only in October 1946.

The Ryotwari settlement, in which revenue was fixed directly with the individual cultivator with no intermediary zamindar, was first worked out by Captain Alexander Read and Thomas Munro in the Baramahal district from 1792 and extended across Madras when Munro became Governor. Cornwallis is the trap — he made the Permanent Settlement instead.

The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's monopoly of Indian trade (keeping tea and the China trade for it) and opened India to private British merchants; the remaining monopoly over tea and China trade went in 1833.

Lord Cornwallis concluded the Permanent Settlement with the zamindars of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1793, fixing the land revenue demand for ever, with the Sunset Law auctioning off estates whose dues were not paid by sunset of the due date.

Henry Vivian Derozio, the Anglo-Indian teacher at Hindu College from 1826, inspired the Young Bengal radicals with rationalism and the French Revolution; he was dismissed in 1831 and died of cholera the same year, aged 22.
Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj at Bombay on 10 April 1875; its headquarters later moved to Lahore, which is why Punjab became the movement's real centre — but the founding city was Bombay.

Raja Ram Mohan Roy set up the Vedanta College in 1825 to teach Indian monotheistic philosophy alongside Western social and physical science; he had earlier helped David Hare found Hindu College (1817) and later established the Brahmo Sabha (1828).

Sir Syed Ahmed Khan founded the United Indian Patriotic Association in 1888, with Raja Shiv Prasad of Benares, to counter the Indian National Congress and persuade Muslims and loyalist Hindus to stay away from it. The Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental Defence Association of Upper India came later, in 1893, and the Muslim League only in 1906.

The sepoys at Meerut rose on 10 May 1857, after 85 of their comrades were court-martialled and jailed on 9 May for refusing the greased cartridges; they marched to Delhi overnight and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar emperor on 11 May.

Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, called Frontier Gandhi or Badshah Khan, built the non-violent Khudai Khidmatgar (Red Shirts) among the Pathans of the North-West Frontier Province from 1929; he received the Bharat Ratna in 1987.

The Charter Act of 1853 ended the Directors' patronage and threw the covenanted civil service open to competitive examination, on Macaulay Committee lines, with the first exam held in 1855 — that is when a civil service proper began. The Charter Act of 1833 is the near-miss: it declared that no Indian should be debarred by religion, birth or colour, but that principle was never given effect.
The Quit India movement was launched on 8 August 1942 at the Bombay AICC session, after the failure of the Cripps Mission earlier that year and with the Japanese at India's eastern door.

The question is defective: a state planning board is chaired ex officio by that state's Chief Minister, yet none of the options is a Mizoram figure. The option set fits the national Planning Commission instead, whose first chairman was Jawaharlal Nehru from 1950, so that is the closest available answer — Mahalanobis was only a member and the statistical architect of the Second Plan.
